name: עַמִּינָדָב
summary: Borne by the man of Judah, son of Ram, whose son Nahshon was prince of Judah and led its host when Israel set out from Sinai, and whose daughter Elisheba married Aaron (Exo 6:23; Num 10:14; Rut 4:19–20); he stands in the line of David and of Jesus (Mat 1:4; Luk 3:33). Also borne by a son of Kohath in the Levites' line (1Ch 6:7, where Exo 6:18 and 1Ch 6:23 have Izhar) and by the chief of the sons of Uzziel who brought up the ark under David (1Ch 15:10–11). It is עַם “people, kinsman” with the ־ִי of “my”, and נָדָב “willing, given freely; noble”: “my kinsman is willing” or “is noble”, the kinsman being God, as in עַמִּיאֵל and עַמִּיהוּד. The Song of Songs has the same two words, עַמִּי־נָדִיב (Sng 6:12).

evidence.note: The standard of the camp of the sons of Judah set out first, and over its host נַחְשׁוֹן בֶּן־עַמִּינָדָב.
Aaron took Elisheba daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon; she bore him נָדָב, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar: the grandson's name repeats the second element.
For Judah, Nahshon son of Amminadab (also Num 2:3; 7:12, 17).
Nahshon son of Amminadab offered first at the dedication of the altar.
Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, in the line to David (also 1Ch 2:10).
Ἀμιναδάβ in the genealogy of Jesus Christ (also Luk 3:33).
The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son; in the parallel lists the son of Kohath and father of Korah is Izhar (Exo 6:18, 21; 1Ch 6:23).
Of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, and his brothers, 112.
David called him with the priests and Levites to bring up the ark.
מַרְכְּבוֹת עַמִּי־נָדִיב, “the chariots of my noble people”: the name's two words, with the adjective.
כֹּל נְדִיב לִבּוֹ, everyone willing of heart: the root's sense, “willing, moved to give”.
Abraham “was gathered to his עַמִּים”: עַם as one's kin.

note: BDB files the name apart (p.dj.am, with no root); it is linked to the nadav entry for its second element, which is spelled as the name נָדָב, not as the adjective נָדִיב: it may be the qal perfect “has been willing, has given freely” (“my kinsman has given freely”) as much as an adjective. The ־ִי may be “my” or a joining vowel. TIPNR gives the Kohathite of 1Ch 6:7 to Izhar@Exo.6.18, whose forms include עַמִּינָדָב, so that record is named here; the bdb key keeps this entry off Izhar's other words. Not checked: the Ammonite king ʿmndb of the Tell Siran bottle and Ashurbanipal's Amminadbi of Bīt-Ammāni, the same name outside Israel; no source for them is in sources.json.
